Photography emerged in the eighteen twenties through eighteen forties as a mechanical process for capturing images through light and chemistry, transforming visual representation from drawn, painted, or sculpted craft into technical reproduction. By fixing light on paper or glass, photography challenged painting's monopoly on depicting reality and established a new artistic medium with its own aesthetic and conceptual possibilities. The technology became foundational to modern visual culture and raised enduring questions about the relationship between mechanical reproduction and artistic truth.

Photography was invented in the eighteen twenties and thirties through experiments by multiple figures working independently. Nicéphore Niépce, Louis Daguerre, and William Fox Talbot each worked to capture light chemically on surfaces. The daguerreotype, developed in eighteen thirty-nine, was the first commercially viable photographic process, producing sharp, detailed silver-copper plates that made portrait photography accessible and popular almost immediately.

Photography displaced painting as the primary vehicle for literal representation and portraiture. Painters responded by abandoning strict realism and exploring subjective color, form, and emotion. This forced liberation shaped modern art's entire trajectory.

The medium united opposites: mechanical objectivity—the camera records what is there—and artistic subjectivity where the photographer frames, lights, and composes. This tension became central to photographic aesthetics. Early photographers adopted painting's compositional language, framing, and subjects to claim artistic legitimacy. Gradual acceptance came as photographers developed distinctly photographic techniques: unusual angles, cropping, depth of field.

Photography enabled new ways of seeing—freeze-framing motion, revealing detail invisible to the naked eye, flattening three-dimensional space into two dimensions—that artists like Degas directly learned from and incorporated into painting. Vision itself was transformed by the camera's capacity to see what human eyes could not.

The medium fragmented into separate traditions: commercial portraiture and documentation, scientific photography for medical and astronomical and archaeological purposes, and artistic fine art photography as modernism. Photography's indexical nature—it records light rays from the real world rather than representing it—gave the medium philosophical weight. It was literal trace, not interpretation, yet paradoxically subject to manipulation at every stage of exposure, development, and printing. Truth and artifice became inseparable in the photographic image.
